video_notes.title: Build an LLM from Scratch 7: Instruction Finetuning
video_notes.contributed: Full from-scratch walkthrough of building an instruction-tuning dataset (Alpaca formatting, batch-level padding, loss masking), running SFT on GPT-2, and an LLM-as-judge evaluation pipeline using a local Ollama model.

video_notes.title: LoRA & QLoRA Explained Simply | Full Fine-Tuning vs PEFT + Intuition + Practical
video_notes.contributed: Conceptual grounding in matrix rank and decomposition that underlies LoRA/QLoRA, a comparison of full fine-tuning vs PEFT methods, and a hands-on Hugging Face PEFT script fine-tuning TinyLlama with LoRA.

video_notes.title: Fine-Tuning LLMs for Real-World Tool Calling: Lessons from tau2-bench
video_notes.contributed: A production-style SFT-then-GRPO fine-tuning workflow for tool-calling reliability, with reward-shaping details, pass^k evaluation, and hard-won lessons on reward hacking and teacher-trace data quality.

video_notes.title: Design with AI - Full Guide (Tools, Workflows, Design Systems)
video_notes.contributed: Nothing on LLM fine-tuning. This talk is about AI-assisted UI/UX design tooling (Figma, Claude/Grok/Codex design workflows, design-system skills) and is off-topic for a fine-tuning build guide.

claims.claim: Convert raw instruction/input/output JSON entries into plain text with the Alpaca-style boilerplate template before feeding them to the model, since LLMs are trained on text, not dictionaries.
claims.quote: this is the alpaka prompt style template

claims.claim: Production LLMs are typically instruction fine-tuned on at least 100,000 examples, far more than the small teaching dataset used in this walkthrough.
claims.quote: nowadays at least 100,000 training examples

claims.claim: Split the instruction dataset 85% train / 10% test / 5% validation.
claims.quote: 85% for training 10% for testing and then the remaining 5%

claims.claim: Pad each training batch independently to its own longest sequence instead of padding the whole dataset to one global max length, to avoid wasting compute on excess padding tokens.
claims.quote: we will pad only to the longest element in each batch

claims.claim: Replace all but one padding token per sequence with the ignore_index (-100, the cross-entropy loss's default ignore value) so the loss skips excess padding, while keeping exactly one padding token so the model learns to emit an end-of-text stop token.
claims.quote: I'm using minus 100 because that's the default value

claims.claim: The 124M-parameter GPT-2 produced unusable, repetitive responses after instruction tuning; stepping up to the 355M version was necessary to get coherent output on a laptop.
claims.quote: I went one model size up

claims.claim: Instruction fine-tuning the 355M GPT-2 model for 2 epochs took about 15 minutes on an M3 MacBook Air CPU, versus roughly 1 minute on an A100 GPU.
claims.quote: with this 355 million model it took about 15 minutes

claims.claim: Two epochs produced a better fine-tuned model than one, but going further starts pushing the model into overfitting territory as training loss drops well below validation loss.
claims.quote: two was better than one

claims.claim: Instruction fine-tuning (SFT) uses exactly the same next-token-prediction cross-entropy loss as pretraining; only the text structure (instruction/input/response fields vs. raw text) differs.
claims.quote: instruction fine-tuning uses exactly the same loss that we used during pre-training

claims.claim: When instruction fine-tuning, reuse the chapter-5 loss-loader (loss over every token) rather than the chapter-6 version (loss on only the last token), since free-form generation needs loss signal across the whole sequence.
claims.quote: please make sure you're using the correct code from chapter 5

claims.claim: Evaluate free-form fine-tuned responses by having a second local LLM (run via Ollama) score each response against the reference answer on a 0-100 scale, since exact-match accuracy doesn't work for open-ended text.
claims.quote: scale from 0 to 100 where 100 is the best score

claims.claim: A small 3B Ollama judge model gave an average score of 51.6/100 across the 110-example test set, and 14 of the 110 responses couldn't even be parsed into a numeric score.
claims.quote: we get an average score of 51.6

claims.claim: A reader-contributed rubric-based judge prompt using a 1-5 scale (instead of 0-100) produced more consistent LLM-judge scores.
claims.quote: it's just using a scale from 1 to 5

claims.claim: As a rule of thumb, bigger and newer judge models give more capable, more reliable evaluations than a small 3B model, often more effective than just tweaking the prompt.
claims.quote: as a rule of thumb the bigger the models usually the better they are

claims.claim: After instruction fine-tuning, LLM providers commonly run an additional optional alignment/preference-tuning step using RLHF or DPO.
claims.quote: there's also often an optional alignment step

claims.theme: DPO avoids a separate reward model
claims.claim: DPO is popular because, unlike RLHF, it skips training a separate reward model — RLHF otherwise requires holding two LLMs in memory at once, raising compute cost.
claims.quote: two llms in your compute memory which is more expensive

claims.claim: Preference/DPO datasets pair a chosen (preferred) response with a rejected response for the same prompt, rather than supplying a single target output.
claims.quote: chosen response could also be called preferred response

claims.claim: Preference tuning is also used to make models refuse harmful requests and cut down on profanity, not just to pick the stylistically 'better' of two valid answers.
claims.quote: making the LM a bit safer in that sense

claims.claim: Terser instruction-formatting styles (like Microsoft Phi-3's, which skips Alpaca's boilerplate) are preferable because generation is token-by-token, so fewer tokens per example means cheaper, faster training and inference.
claims.quote: shorter and shorter is cheaper

claims.claim: When building an instruction dataset, deduplicate near-duplicate entries to avoid wasting training time on redundant examples.
claims.quote: I made a few examples and then I found near duplicates removed them

claims.claim: Fine-tuning results differ slightly across CPU, Apple MPS, and GPU backends, and even across PyTorch versions, so don't expect bit-identical outputs when switching hardware or library versions.
claims.quote: right now in 2.6 the results are very close between CPU and GPU

claims.claim: The full LLM training pipeline has three stages: pretraining on internet-scale data, instruction fine-tuning to teach custom behavior, and preference alignment to match human preferences.
claims.quote: the first stage of this training pipeline is called the pre-training

claims.claim: You can take a model after any pipeline stage — base, instruct-tuned, or preference-aligned — and run your own custom fine-tuning on top of it.
claims.quote: after any stage we can pick up the LLM model and we can perform

claims.claim: Full fine-tuning updates every model weight, so a 7B model means 7B trainable weights, a 13B model means 13B trainable weights, scaling costs linearly with model size.
claims.quote: if you have 13 billion model, then you have 13 billion weights

claims.theme: Full fine-tuning is impractical at scale
claims.claim: Full-parameter fine-tuning requires large GPUs or GPU clusters and isn't a practical choice for most teams, which is why parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods emerged.
claims.quote: full parameter fine-tuning is not a practical choice

claims.claim: Beyond LoRA, parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods include DoRA, QLoRA, prefix tuning, prompt tuning, BitFit, IA3, and plain adapters — though interviewers mostly only probe LoRA and QLoRA.
claims.quote: LoRA adaptation is a very famous method to achieve this PEFT

claims.claim: LoRA's practical payoff is less memory use, faster training, lower cost, easy customization, and single-GPU fine-tuning with performance that stays close to full fine-tuning.
claims.quote: less memory, faster training, lower cost, and the easy customization

claims.claim: A matrix's rank is the number of linearly independent rows (or columns) it has — this is the exact property LoRA exploits to decompose large weight matrices into small trainable ones.
claims.quote: number of linearly independent rows and columns

claims.claim: A rank-2, 4x5 weight matrix (20 parameters) can be factored into a 4x2 and a 2x5 matrix (8+10=18 parameters) that multiply back to the same matrix — the arithmetic basis for LoRA's parameter savings, which compounds dramatically at billion-parameter scale.
claims.quote: so, in total we have 18 parameter

claims.claim: LoRA freezes the original weight matrix W0 and learns two small matrices, A and B, whose product is added on top; only A and B get trained.
claims.quote: decompose uh this actual weight matrix uh which is W into two

claims.claim: On GPT-3 (~175B parameters), full fine-tuning retrains roughly all 175 billion weights, while LoRA trains only about 4.7 million parameters for the same task.
claims.quote: we are just going to be trained only 4.7 million of parameter

claims.claim: Per the cited benchmark numbers, full fine-tuning reached 89.5% accuracy while LoRA matched or slightly exceeded it despite training a tiny fraction of the parameters.
claims.quote: we were getting 89.5% accuracy

claims.claim: QLoRA is LoRA plus quantization: the frozen base weights are loaded in 4-bit precision to cut memory further, while LoRA full-precision is used when memory isn't the bottleneck.
claims.quote: we are going to be use the 4-bit, right, the quantized model

claims.claim: Tasks that would otherwise need 24GB+ of VRAM can often run on just 8-16GB thanks to QLoRA's 4-bit quantization.
claims.quote: 8 to 16 GB will be enough for the respective task

claims.claim: Because the base model stays frozen, you can keep multiple LoRA adapters for different tasks and swap between them without duplicating the full model weights.
claims.quote: different LoRA adapter for a multiple task without duplicating the full model

claims.claim: Transformer/LLM training typically uses AdamW rather than plain Adam or SGD, because it layers in weight decay alongside a learning-rate scheduler and warmup.
claims.quote: it's going to be combine this weight decay concept

claims.theme: Required packages for a LoRA run
claims.claim: A Hugging Face LoRA fine-tuning setup needs transformers, datasets, peft, accelerate, bitsandbytes (for quantization), and trl (for SFT/preference-tuning training loops).
claims.quote: data set, peft, accelerator, bits and bytes, TRL

claims.claim: The hands-on demo fine-tunes TinyLlama (1.1B parameters) with LoRA on a small slice of an English-quotes dataset.
claims.quote: model name is a tiny llama and the model parameter is 1.1 billion

claims.claim: After wrapping TinyLlama with the LoRA config (rank 16, alpha 32) via get_peft_model, only about 0.277% of total parameters are actually trainable.
claims.quote: it is just uh 0.277 of this all the parameter

claims.claim: After LoRA training, merge the adapter weights into the base model to produce a single standalone model for inference instead of shipping base weights and adapter separately.
claims.quote: merge the Laura adapter with that previous model only

claims.claim: Rising production AI inference costs are pushing teams toward fine-tuning open-source models instead of relying solely on closed frontier APIs.
claims.quote: AI inference cost has been gaining scrutiny

claims.claim: A closed model like GPT-4.1 mini can cost roughly 4-5x more per task than a comparable open-source alternative.
claims.quote: actually four or five times more expensive than open source model

claims.claim: The case study fine-tunes the open-source Qwen3 30B model specifically to make it more reliable at calling tools.
claims.quote: fine-tune, right, Qwen 3 30B parameters on a specific task

claims.claim: Task success in tau2-bench is judged by checking the resulting environment state (e.g., did a customer's data allowance actually increase by 2GB), not by scoring the conversation text itself.
claims.quote: whether for this particular task data actually increased by 2 GB

claims.claim: Multi-turn user-agent conversations are logged as rollouts in Weights & Biases to build the trace dataset later used for SFT and RL.
claims.quote: we basically log the traces of the interaction between the user and

claims.claim: The fine-tuning workflow is staged: supervised fine-tuning on teacher-generated trajectories first, then reinforcement learning with GRPO to push performance further.
claims.quote: try to push the performance further by use by doing reinforcement learning

claims.claim: Supervised fine-tuning ran on Weights & Biases' serverless SFT offering; the RL stage used the OpenPipe SDK on self-managed H100 GPUs.
claims.quote: I'm actually using Weights & Biases uh serverless uh supervised fine-tuning

claims.claim: A teacher model (GLM) solved 68 of 74 designed tasks when generating candidate SFT trajectories for distillation.
claims.quote: it actually able to solve 68 of the 74 tasks

claims.claim: Of roughly 822 raw rollouts collected, only 669 'clean' trajectories (filtered for efficiency and absence of hallucinated tool calls) were kept for supervised fine-tuning.
claims.quote: to use 669 clean trajectories, right, for the uh supervised fine-tuning

claims.claim: The GRPO reward combines multiple signals — action fraction (tool-call recall), a termination bonus, tool-name accuracy, tool-argument accuracy, and a step penalty — rather than a single pass/fail signal.
claims.quote: the first one is action fraction

claims.claim: Weighting reward components evenly let the model learn to repeatedly call a correct-but-redundant tool (e.g., re-fetching customer ID) just to farm the action-fraction reward instead of finishing the task; the fix was upweighting task completion.
claims.quote: there's actually presence of reward reward hacking

claims.claim: Evaluate tool-calling reliability with pass^k (success required k consecutive times), which is far stricter than pass^1 and exposes consistency problems a single successful run would hide.
claims.quote: pass three itself, right? It's significantly lower than pass one

claims.claim: SFT alone lifted the model's pass^3 score from ~37.5% to 75%; adding GRPO-based RL pushed it incrementally further, to 77.5%, beating the closed GPT-4.1 mini baseline at lower cost.
claims.quote: from 37.5, right? Increased to 75 percent percentage

claims.claim: The team benchmarked against GPT-4.1 mini specifically because it predates the tau2-bench dataset's release, reducing the risk the closed model had already seen the benchmark.
claims.quote: it was um released after GPT 4.1 mini

claims.claim: Teams typically optimize for performance first with closed models, then once productionizing, evaluate open-source fine-tuning for cost — often ending up with a tiered setup where frontier models handle hard tasks and fine-tuned small models handle simpler ones.
claims.quote: break their workload into final workload

claims.claim: Training a student model on unverified teacher-generated SFT traces is risky: some trajectories pass the success metric while actually hallucinating tool calls or succeeding by luck, and that noise propagates into later RL training, making it unstable.
claims.quote: a lot of the RL roll out trajectories are actually hallucinating a lot

claims.claim: Mitigate noisy teacher traces by adding programmatic checks in the SFT stage — e.g., flagging tool-not-found errors or checking response tone — before trajectories get used to train the RL stage.
claims.quote: more programmatic evaluation or got reals in your SFT stage

claims.theme: Silent failures are hard to catch
claims.claim: Tool-calling agents can fail silently on either side of an interaction — e.g., a user never enabling app permissions, or the agent never enabling roaming — with no explicit error signal, making these failures especially hard to detect in evaluation.
claims.quote: it needs to enable the roaming uh on the agent side

disagreements.topic: Is full-parameter fine-tuning a reasonable default, or should PEFT always be preferred?

positions.position: Raschka fully fine-tunes GPT-2 (355M) end-to-end for the book's instruction-tuning chapter, treating full fine-tuning as the default teaching path at small scale (even picking a bigger base model rather than reaching for LoRA when results were weak).

Sunny Savita argues full-parameter fine-tuning 'is not a practical choice' in general, and frames LoRA/QLoRA as the default even for modest setups, since full fine-tuning's memory and compute cost scale directly with model size.

disagreements.topic: Which alignment method is better, RLHF or DPO?

positions.position: Raschka says 'the jury is still out' on which performs better; DPO is simpler to implement (no separate reward model) but may trade off some modeling performance versus RLHF, which is why both remain in use.

disagreements.topic: Is passing a task's success metric sufficient evidence that a training trajectory is good?

positions.position: Raschka's evaluation approach scores finished responses after the fact with an LLM judge (0-100 or 1-5 scale), implicitly treating a good final-answer score as sufficient evidence of quality.

The TMLS talk explicitly warns that passing the task's success metric is not sufficient — trajectories can pass while hallucinating tool calls or succeeding by luck — and recommends programmatic guardrails during SFT data curation, not just outcome scoring.

gaps: None of the four videos give concrete dollar-cost figures for a full fine-tuning or LoRA/QLoRA training run on cloud GPUs — only wall-clock minutes and token counts are reported.
No guidance on fine-tuning multimodal or vision-language models; all examples are text-only LLMs.
No walkthrough of concrete hyperparameter values (learning rate schedule, warmup steps, weight decay) for AdamW in a production fine-tuning run — AdamW is named but not tuned on-screen.
No coverage of distributed or multi-GPU fine-tuning; both the from-scratch SFT demo and the LoRA demo run on a single machine (a MacBook Air or one Colab/H100 GPU).
No discussion of continued/domain-adaptive pretraining as a step before instruction fine-tuning.
The TMLS talk doesn't disclose exact GRPO hyperparameters (group size, KL penalty coefficient, learning rate) or the total training duration/cost of the RL stage.
No guidance on how to actually choose a LoRA rank or alpha value beyond 'it's a hyperparameter you can check out' — no systematic selection method is given.
No discussion of safety/red-teaming evaluation of fine-tuned models beyond a passing mention that preference tuning can reduce swearing or harmful outputs.
r-MPiu0E4W4 ('Design with AI') contains no fine-tuning content at all — it covers AI-assisted UI/UX design tooling and workflows, so it cannot answer any build questions about fine-tuning LLMs.
